bodyHtml:
Why marketing is hard for an NDT company

Most NDT companies do not have a marketing department. They have an owner who is also a Level III, a business development person who spends half the week on site visits, and an office manager who does the newsletter when there is time. There rarely is.

The result is predictable. The last client newsletter went out so long ago nobody remembers it. The people who stopped at your stand at the last trade show never heard from you again. The fabrication shop that asked about MT and PT in the spring and went quiet was never contacted again. Your new phased array capability, the one you invested heavily in equipment and training for, was announced once and then forgotten.

It is not a lack of things to say. NDT companies know a lot that their clients would find useful: what changed in a code edition, when to use TOFD instead of RT, why a PAUT scan plan matters, what a technician's certification actually covers. The problem is time. Writing a good email takes an engineer an hour they do not have.

The AI Marketing app in the Atlantis NDT ERP is built to close that gap. It drafts campaign emails with AI from a short brief, runs drip sequences by service line, and schedules sends, so marketing happens steadily in the background instead of in rare bursts. You stay in control of what goes out. The AI writes the first draft; your expertise decides what is right.

If that sounds like the gap in your business, book an AI Marketing demo and we will show you a campaign drafted for an NDT audience.

Four kinds of campaign email, drafted by AI

AI Marketing generates campaign emails in four types. Each suits a different job in an NDT company's marketing.

Newsletter

A regular update to clients and prospects: a capability you have added, a short technical explainer, upcoming training intakes, a reminder of the services you offer. Newsletters keep your name in front of maintenance planners and inspection engineers between jobs, so you are the first call when a shutdown scope lands.

Promotion

A focused message about one service: phased array weld inspection for fabrication shops, tank floor inspection ahead of a planned outage, a training course with seats left. Promotions work best sent to a narrow, relevant list.

Nurture

Educational emails for people who are not ready to buy yet. A nurture email might explain how to write a clear inspection scope, what information an NDT company needs to quote accurately, or how Level I, II and III responsibilities differ. Nurture builds trust with the engineers who will specify the work.

Announcement

News that deserves its own email: a new method added to your services, a new region covered, a new accreditation for your company, a new training programme, or a new way of delivering reports.

For each type, you give the AI a brief: who it is for, which service line it concerns and the key points. It returns a draft with a subject line and body. You then edit it, check every technical statement, and schedule or send. The draft is yours to change completely; the AI saves you the blank page, not the judgement.

How AI drafting works in practice

Here is a realistic example. Your operations manager mentions that the crew calendar looks light in a few weeks' time, and you want to fill it with MT and PT work from local fabrication shops.

  1. You open AI Marketing and choose a promotion email.
  2. You write a short brief: the audience is fabrication shop QA managers and production managers; the service is MT and PT on structural and pressure welds; the points are short-notice availability, qualified technicians, clear reports and a link to send a scope.
  3. The AI drafts a subject line and body in plain language.
  4. You read it. You remove a line that overstates your turnaround, add the procedure standard your clients usually ask about, and tighten the call to action.
  5. You send a test to yourself, check it on your phone, then schedule it for your fabrication shop list on Tuesday morning.

The job takes minutes instead of an afternoon, and the final email still says what you would have said yourself.

A few rules make AI drafting work in a technical industry:

  • Brief it with facts. The AI writes from what you give it. Give it your real methods, sectors and service areas.
  • Check every technical claim. A Level III or senior technician should read anything that mentions codes, acceptance criteria or techniques.
  • Never let it invent results. Remove any figures, percentages or client names that you cannot back up. Engineers notice.
  • Keep your voice. Edit the draft until it sounds like your company, not like a brochure.
  • Keep it short. Site engineers read email on their phones between jobs. Three tight paragraphs and one clear action beat a page of text.

AI that can run on your own server

Many NDT companies are wary of sending client information to outside AI services, and with good reason. Your client list, the sites you work at and the scopes you quote are commercially sensitive. Some of your clients may have contract clauses about how their information is handled.

AI Marketing uses an AI model that can run on your own server. That means drafting can happen on infrastructure you control, with your campaign briefs and contact details staying inside it. Where the model runs and which model is used is agreed with you during implementation, based on your hardware, your privacy requirements and the quality of drafts you need.

Running a model on your own server has practical trade-offs worth discussing openly:

  • It needs a machine with enough capacity to run the model at a usable speed.
  • Smaller models are faster but produce plainer drafts; larger models write better but need more hardware.
  • You are not dependent on an outside AI service being available, or on its terms changing.

Whatever you choose, the principle stays the same. The AI produces drafts. People in your company decide what is sent. Nothing about the AI removes the need for someone who understands NDT to read an email before it reaches a client.

The same approach applies to the AI-personalised email preview in the CRM app, where a salesperson generates a tailored follow-up for a single lead, reads it and edits it before sending. Nothing leaves without a person pressing send or deliberately enrolling a lead in a sequence.

Drip sequences by service line

A drip sequence is a series of emails sent to a contact over time, on a schedule you set, until they reply, buy or opt out. It is the most reliable way to stay in touch with the many leads who are genuinely interested but not ready yet.

In AI Marketing, drip sequences are organised by service line. That matters because an NDT company's audiences want very different things.

Inspection sequence

For plant engineers, maintenance planners and fabrication QA managers. A typical sequence might introduce your methods and sectors, explain how to prepare a scope for a quick and accurate quote, show what your reports include, and close with an invitation to discuss an upcoming outage. You can also mention that results can be placed on a 3D model of the asset with Digital Twin Reporting Software, Atlantis's companion product to the ERP's NDT Reports app.

Training sequence

For individuals and training coordinators. It might cover course levels and methods, what practical time looks like, how learners prepare between sessions, and upcoming intake dates.

Consulting sequence

For QA/QC managers and engineering leads. It might cover procedure writing and review, Level III services, supplier audits and reviews of a written practice.

Leads can be enrolled from the CRM with one action, so a salesperson who qualifies a nurture lead can hand it to the right sequence in seconds. Each sequence is drafted once with the AI's help, reviewed by the right people, and then runs on its schedule while your team gets on with the work.

Pause, resume and unsubscribe

Automation without an off switch is how companies end up annoying their best prospects. AI Marketing gives you three controls on drip sequences.

  • Pause: stop the sequence without losing its place. Useful when a lead picks up the phone and becomes a live opportunity, or when a client is in the middle of a shutdown and does not need marketing email.
  • Resume: carry on from where it stopped when the time is right.
  • Unsubscribe: recipients can opt out, and they stop receiving the sequence.

These controls reflect how NDT sales actually works. A nurture lead who replies 'we have an outage in the spring, call me in January' should not receive three more generic emails before January. Pause, schedule an activity in the CRM for January, and resume later with something relevant.

Respecting opt-outs is also part of your legal and reputational obligations. The industry is small; the inspection engineer irritated by your emails today may be the contractor's QA manager next year. Privacy and marketing rules differ by country, so what consent you need before adding someone to a sequence is a decision for you and your advisers. The ERP helps you record and honour those choices.

A good rule of thumb: every email in a sequence should be one the recipient would be glad to receive even if they never buy from you. If an email fails that test, rewrite it or cut it.

Scheduling around the NDT calendar

Timing matters in this industry more than most. Scheduling lets you prepare campaigns in advance and send them when they are most likely to be read and acted on.

  • Shutdown and turnaround season. Plants plan outages months ahead. Inspection promotions sent while scopes are being written are far more useful than ones sent after contracts are awarded.
  • Training intakes. Announce course dates early enough for employers to approve budgets and release people from site.
  • Trade shows and conferences. Send a 'meet us at the stand' email before the event, and a follow-up afterwards to the people you met, many of whom you can capture on the day with the Business Cards app.
  • Quiet periods. If your crew calendar looks light, a scheduled promotion to the right list can help fill it.
  • Working hours and time zones. If you work across several countries, schedule so emails land in the morning where the recipient is.

A simple content calendar goes a long way. Plan a regular newsletter, a handful of promotions a year aligned with your busy and quiet seasons, announcements when you have genuine news, and drip sequences running continuously in the background. Draft a few weeks ahead with the AI, review in one sitting, and schedule.

That turns marketing from something that happens when there is time into a steady routine one person can manage alongside their other work.

What to write about: topics NDT buyers actually read

The AI can draft quickly, but it needs good subjects. These are topics that inspection engineers, QA/QC managers and plant planners tend to find useful, as long as you write them from real experience.

  • Method selection: when UT is a better choice than RT, what TOFD adds, where phased array saves access time, what ET is good at on tubing.
  • Preparing a scope: the information an NDT company needs to quote accurately, such as drawings, material, thickness, weld count, access and applicable code.
  • Reading a report: what an inspection report should contain, and what 'acceptable with remarks' means for the person receiving it.
  • Technician qualification: what Level I, II and III can and cannot do, and why the certification scheme on a technician's card matters to the client.
  • Procedures: why a written, approved procedure matters and what a Level III looks for when reviewing one.
  • New ways of presenting results: how inspection results placed on a 3D model of an asset help plant teams see where findings cluster across a unit.
  • Training: how learners build practical skill between classroom sessions. Learners enrolled in the ERP's eLearning portal get access to Practical NDT, Atlantis's immersive 3D practice platform with UT, PAUT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET and TOFD scenarios on virtual welds, pipes, vessels and castings. That is worth an announcement of its own.

Avoid the things that make technical readers stop reading: vague claims, invented statistics, and anything that sounds like it was written by someone who has never been on a scaffold. Specific, useful and short wins every time.

Who uses AI Marketing

  • Owner or managing director: sets the themes, approves the tone and reviews key announcements.
  • Business development: writes briefs, reviews drafts, enrols leads into sequences and pauses them when leads go live.
  • Office manager or marketing coordinator: runs the calendar, schedules sends and keeps lists in order.
  • NDT Level III: technical review of anything that mentions methods, codes or acceptance criteria.
  • Training coordinator: training sequences and intake announcements.

In a small company these may be two or three people. The point of AI Marketing is that none of them needs to be a professional copywriter. They need to know the work, write a clear brief and read critically.

Access rights decide who can create campaigns, who can edit sequences and who can send. Many companies let several people draft but limit sending to one or two, so nothing reaches a client list without a second look.

A simple routine keeps it running: drafts are created through the week as ideas come up, reviewed together in one short session, then scheduled. Sequences are checked every few months to retire anything out of date, such as old course dates or a service you no longer offer.

How AI Marketing connects to the rest of the ERP

  • CRM: leads carry service line, sector, NDT service type and a lead score from 0 to 100 banded hot, warm, nurture or cold. Nurture leads are natural candidates for drip sequences and can be enrolled from the lead.
  • Contacts: the shared address book of clients, prospects, learners and partners your campaigns reach.
  • Email Marketing: Odoo's standard mass mailing app, with mailing lists, an email editor and open and click tracking. Both apps work from the same contacts. See the Email Marketing app.
  • Business Cards: cards photographed at a trade show become CRM leads or mailing list members, ready for the post-event follow-up.
  • Website: enquiry forms create CRM leads, which can then be enrolled in the right sequence.
  • Quotations: when a nurture lead finally asks for a price, the opportunity moves to a quotation in the same system.

Because everything shares one database, the lead a salesperson qualifies, the sequence it enters and the quotation it becomes are all visible in the same place. Nobody has to export a list from one tool and import it into another, and nobody has to wonder whether the client already heard from you this week.

Setup and implementation

Atlantis NDT deploys and configures the ERP for you. For AI Marketing, the work usually covers:

  1. Where the AI runs: on your own server or another option agreed with you, and which model suits your hardware and the quality of drafts you need.
  2. Outgoing email: sending from your own domain, set up with the authentication mail providers expect so campaigns are less likely to land in spam.
  3. Service lines: the inspection, training and consulting lines your sequences follow.
  4. First sequences: an initial drip sequence for each service line, drafted with you and reviewed by your Level III.
  5. Lists and segments: connecting Contacts, CRM fields and mailing lists.
  6. Training: writing good briefs, reviewing drafts, scheduling, pausing and resuming.

Anything specific to your company, such as an approval step before sending, is part of the customization scope agreed with you. The Atlantis NDT ERP is affordable, accessible and fully customizable, and pricing is quote on request. See every app in the system on the ERP apps page.

Frequently asked questions

Does the AI send emails without anyone checking?

No. The AI drafts; a person reviews, edits and schedules or sends. Automated sending only happens through drip sequences you have set up and deliberately enrolled leads into, and those can be paused at any time.

Where does the AI model run?

AI Marketing uses a model that can run on your own server, so briefs and contact details can stay on infrastructure you control. The exact setup is agreed during implementation.

What types of email can it draft?

Four campaign types: newsletter, promotion, nurture and announcement. You brief it on audience, service line and key points, and it returns a subject line and body for you to edit.

Can we run different sequences for inspection, training and consulting?

Yes. Drip sequences are organised by service line, so each audience gets content that fits what they asked about.

What happens when a lead replies or becomes a live opportunity?

Pause their sequence and hand the lead to a salesperson in the CRM. You can resume later if the timing is not right yet.

Is the AI reliable on technical content?

Treat every draft as a draft. The AI can phrase things well but can also get technical details wrong, so anything about methods, codes or acceptance criteria should be checked by a Level III or senior technician.

What does it cost?

Pricing depends on your users, apps and customization scope, so it is by quote on request.
